read.passage: In competitive debating, winning is rarely about having the most arguments. Judges look instead at how well each team engages with the other side. A strong rebuttal does not simply deny an opponent's claim; it exposes the assumption on which that claim rests, or shows that the evidence points the other way. Equally important is weighing. Even when a team concedes that its opponents have made a fair point, it can still win by explaining why its own arguments matter more, because the harm it describes is larger, more likely or irreversible. Finally, the reply speech should introduce no new material. Its purpose is to crystallise the key clashes and show, calmly and precisely, where the opposition fell short. Many experienced judges say that debates are won not in the first speech, but in the last.
